Sound Storm Labs SMC90BB Sound System Weatherproof Bluetooth Amplifier 3 Inch Speakers Inline Volume Control Ideal for Motorcycles ATV and 12 Volt Applications My husband put this on one of the farm Polaris CUV's since installation is beyond what I would able to do. He was able to install it on a ranger using the roof system as the mounting position for the speakers. It installed easily enough - basically clamp the speaker to the roof support bars, make sure to use the included rubber strips to get these to clamp securely or you will be remounting these with the rubber strips again once they slide down. Wiring was simple as it all goes to one plug that attaches to the amp. This does mean you will be mounting all 4 speakers. And since the wiring is together in a harness, some thought is required as to where you put the speakers and a good route to where you want the amp installed. The amp install is simple as it basically needs power (12vdc) and not a lot else. It does come with a handy audio input jack so you can use something like an old iPod for audio input. It also has BNC inputs if you have say a radio that you would want to connect to it so there is some flexibility there. The Bluetooth hook up was simple and works well, but again do not hide the amp behind a lot of metal or this may not work to well.

As far as fit and finish, the only thing I can knock this on is the quality of the clamping hardware finish, but being on a rough duty vehicle this is actually okay.

The bottom line is: Overall installation is simple, and the unit is easy to use.
text_fidelity_b: Sound Storm Labs SMC90BB Sound System Weatherproof Bluetooth Amplifier 3 Inch Speakers Inline Volume Control Ideal for Motorcycles ATV and 12 Volt Applications

text_fidelity_a: Fire TV Cube (1st Gen), hands-free with Alexa and 4K Ultra HD and 2nd Gen Alexa Voice Remote - Previous Generation 1st off, I do like the voice input and the remote works well. That said, it is not setup for an environment where there are multiple inputs to, in my case, my Denon HEOS AVR.  Fire Cube, Blu-Ray, and cable box each have an input in the AVR with one output to the TV. The Fire TV Cube can't deal with that; during set up it asks me to choose input name by label when setting up an activity, eg: Blu-ray, cable box, etc.  None of them work. My Harmony hub, knows my Denon and lets me designate HDMI 4 for Fire Cube, HDMI 2 for Blu-ray, etc.  I have to use the Denon HEOS app to switch the inputs on the AVR if I want to switch from Fire TV Cube streaming to my cable box or Blu-Ray player.  Not a biggie...mostly I stream, but Amazon really ought to have a better data base of components, as Logitech does with their Harmony products. text_fidelity_a: YYK Bone Conduction Headphones On-Ear Earbuds Built-in Noise-Canceling Mic,IPX7 Waterproof Sports Wireless Earphones Bluetooth Headphones for Workout Running Red My husband works out and I recently (accidentally) washed his workout shorts with his earbuds in the pockets. Of course it was his fault for leaving them in there, but I felt some guilt, so when offered, I ordered these as a replacement. This review is based on his experiences: The Bone Conduction Sports Bluetooth headset was very comfortable (in the ear). Connecting it to a phone was very easy. It comes with everything you need: a manual, charging cable, and an extra set of earbud covers/caps for different ear sizes. You can control/adjust the volume and skip songs via a control (push button) on the earpiece. Even while running, they felt secure. And finally, his only hesitation in giving this product 5 stars is the ability to hear outside noise. He feels that this is a result of how the earbuds are designed. Unlike other headsets he has owned in the past, these sit “outside” of the ear canal/not directly in the ear, which means you do lose some sound quality. Perhaps, if these buds fit inside the ear a little deeper, or you use a headband to press the earbuds closer, the sound quality would improve. In conclusion, he believes these earbuds are not “bad,” especially at this price point ($50 on Amazon), but it could be improved. 4 stars

Its reading is way off for me - as confirmed by a pulse ox and manually counting. The watch kept telling me my heart rate was over 100 just around the house. I have nsvt but my heart rate generally runs low. So I'm very sensitive when I have palpitations - when this watch kept saying my heart rate was over 95 I wasnt buying it. That brings into question any other readings or parameters.

I find the watch annoying and frustrating to use. The watch face does not interact very well for me. I'm constantly trying to tap it and it wont register so then the screen shuts off. Another annoying thing is it tells you to start moving around when I'm doing housework. I guess you can shut that off but I've really lost interest. Hopefully Garmin can offer some fix for the reading since its past the return date.

The positives - watch is comfortable and I don't wear jewelry. I forget its on. Its a large size so its readable if you have vision issues. I've had no problem with that.

text_fidelity_a:
Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White I ordered a three pack because I wanted one for my music room, living room and one for my girlfriend. Set up was super simple for the basics - connecting to a bluetooth speaker, your calendar (I use google's calendar), and a music source. For the latter I use Pandora and that, too, was simple.

The subtracted star is because while I own a few thousand dollars worth of MP3 albums that I purchased from Amazon, I cannot access them. Apparently you can only stream music from Amazon's cloud if you have Prime, and even then I am not sure that you can access any of your own music that resides in their cloud. To me that is a fail, and an indication that the business and requirements analysts who assisted in the development of this device do not fully understand customer requirements at a very basic level. Another nit is the iHeart Radio music source that is plain confusing to use.

Some other areas where this would be a LOT more useful is to have the ability to set up more than one route for traffic (currently I can only identify a single route, home-to-work or back, whereas I am frequently traveling from one place to the other and traffic conditions for those trips would be very helpful. The same for the calendar: you can get all events for a single day, but not for a week, or weekend so you still have to fire up a calendar app on your phone, tablet or computer if you want to get a sense of how busy you will be over a period longer than a day.

Still, for fifty bucks each - plus the discount for purchasing a three pack - this is a decent device that has proven to be surprisingly useful in my home. My girlfriend instantly took to hers too. In the week or so that I have been using it I find that I am growing increasingly dependent on mine for streaming music from Pandora, looking up quick information while I am reading or watching a documentary, and letting me know what is on my calendar for a specific day.

I have one of mine connected via bluetooth to a [[ASIN:B019PGACR0 LD Systems MAUI 5 Channel PA System]], and my girlfriend has hers connected to a [[ASIN:B00W8O6MJO Creative Sound Blaster Roar 2 Portable NFC Bluetooth Speaker]], both of which greatly out perform the larger Echo. However I also use my other Dot with just its integrated speaker and it is more than adequate, even for streaming music since I have it on an end table.

Overall, for the current fifty bucks this is a bargain (warts notwithstanding), and while I purchased mine more out of curiosity all three have proven to be useful and practical.
text_fidelity_b: Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White

Amped REC15A Wireless High Power Compact 802.11AC Wi-Fi Range Extender Among the wireless extenders, I have used, this model from Amped has been the easiest to set up, and it works as good as advertised. Using an iPad, it took less than 5 minutes to set up. Very intuitive and well-thought through interface for setting up with very clear information on each screen (an accurate countdown warns you exactly when to expect next steps, etc.). Overall, this has been the most pleasant experience in setting up any electronics gadget that is device-agnostic.

The performance is excellent; in a far away sunroom, the extender easily resulted in a "full" indicator for WiFi devices, and the ethernet port enabled to connect a gaming device (for very infrequent use, this will work very well; I already have an extended port to connect to the TV). The extender has performed consistently as well, no pauses in video streaming, for example.

There is one minor disadvantage, other than what seems to be a tad pricey - the bulk of the unit. It is difficult to place this in plug points with tight corners or abutting walls. I have had mixed experience in trying to print from a device connected to the extended network to a printer on the original network (need to verify settings and will update the review). Overall, an excellent choice for an extender+port option that is extremely easy to set up and works consistently.

I just so happened to have had a need for the smaller size (6" or less) zip ties to secure some corners on a multi tier wire crate. I ratcheted them tight and trimmed off the excess. Not on the posts (need 10-12" ties for that), but to hold together the overlap going from one roll or piece to the next. Since a section of netting always gets blown apart at some point during the winter, I just head out with a handful of zip ties and put it back together again. So yeh, 500 seems like a lot, but when you have them you need a bunch of them.

The 6 inch size is also great for wire management in general, and just about any small sized securing needs.

No complaints. Happy to have them!

Sangean BB-100 BlueBox AM/FM Ultra-Rugged Digital Receiver with Bluetooth, Blue, 12.4" I've had this for several months now. This is a VERY basic radio, which is what I was looking for but here's my + & -'s.
+ The sounds is strong so it works well with a crowd or in noisy places.
+ I only listen to a few stations so having only 5 preset buttons is perfect.
+ I am not rough with anything but this seems to be a heavy duty exterior, able to withstand some accidental knocking around.
+ This radio has the option to use batteries which makes it nice to bring camping or if you have a booth where you sell stuff, etc...
- The antennae is not adjustable which means if you want a clear station you may not get to point the speaker in the direction you prefer, but you have to move the entire radio around to get a clear signal.
- The only adjustments other than "on & off" are volume & station, again, VERY basic features which is fine, but it would be nice to be able to turn down the bass a little. I'm one of those people who like to hear the actual words of a song along with talk radio or sermons, not just feel the beat of the drum or the hard consonants such as "k, d, p & t". ;)

text_fidelity_a:
Contour +2 - Old Packaging (Discontinued by Manufacturer) This is a really cool camera in a lot of ways, and yet there are two things about it that I hate:

1) It writes *.mov files. Why would any company choose that over so many great standards out there? Quicktime is the norm for *.mov files, with other players claiming to play them, but often with issues. Quicktime is one of those programs that - even after you uninstall it and delete everything you can find associated with it in your registry - will hound you until the end of your days to upgrade and constantly ask permission to take over your computer, will change other file extensions to play on it without asking, etc. Therefore, I so loathe Quicktime that I generally won't even touch an *.mov file.

I'd even be tempted to take the product down to three stars because of this, but there is some chance that this was the only format that would allow them to include the GPS data. I sort of doubt it because Apple (Quicktime) is the most ridiculously proprietary company I can think of, but I guess I need to give Contour the benefit of the doubt. Same benefit of the doubt used for annoyance #2:

2) You need to install more software to see the GPS data. I hate installing more and more software on my computer because everything installed is just another chance to have something running as a service or process all the time, wasting your resources. In general, all software is more "bloated" than ever these days, making our more powerful than before computers unable to perform better than before.

I also wish for some Blackberry support, but they might have some with BB OS 10, supposedly. Frankly, I'm not that interested in the smart phone features; they just slow you down.

As I said, the camera is really cool, though, for its ease of use and its mounts. It's obviously geared toward adventurers and people that want to roll off roofs in shopping carts like that one show that used to be popular. It has a great feel to it in its construction and durability, but I want to make clear the very big caveat that these are the only reasons you want this camera. Besides the annoyances mentioned above, I have a couple point and shoot cameras that do 1080p video just as well (actually better, given their native formats) and they are smaller and cost less. But it is pretty awesome to mount this on your bike for those "just in case" scenarios.
text_fidelity_b: Contour +2 - Old Packaging (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a:
NVIDIA Shield TV | 4K HDR Streaming Media Player The world's first all-in-one Plex box, the Shield comes w/ an unlockable (free) Plex Server inside --and not just another client/player like all other consoles. For those of us w/ a LOT of media, Plex is the pinnacle of enjoying your own media with the best interface possible (and it's free); whereas KODI is the best way for streaming media from the internet. The Shield recognized my old archives instantly, and also when I plugged in a USB3 SanDisk flash drive for extra space. I've had 3 WDTVs, 2 Nexus Players, and 1 MiBox, and I wasted all of that time and money until I got this. I've KODI Phoenix and Exodus for internet streaming, and Plex for my 200 movies, 25 seasons of TV shows, 75 instructional videos (on guitar, magic, and yoga), 6k songs, and all my family albums and artwork. I have the Plex client (player) for TV, phones/tablets, XBox 360, Chromebooks, and Chromebox.

The Shield has BOTH the Play Store and the NVidia Store on its dashboard. I can play all my games again because this console doesn't stutter and freeze up. I'd missed my Asphalt 8 when the others just couldn't handle the workload anymore. I can get even better games from the NVidia Store that the Play Sore doesn't have. Of course, all previous purchases come right back to the Shield --like the HomeRun HD. Plex has a deal they're making w/ HomeRun HD to possibly turn the shield into also doing DVR.

The gamepad has been totally redesigned and has gone from an Ugly Duckling to being prettier than a pail full of kittens. The hex-grip feels good in the hand for shooting zombies or driving on racetracks. The gamepad is rechargeable (yay!) and even comes w/ it's own charging cable. The once $50-extra remote is now included w/ the console. Like the gamepad, the remote also has a headphone jack for discreet listening and a touchscreen volume control and Mute.
text_fidelity_b: NVIDIA Shield TV | 4K HDR Streaming Media Player

text_fidelity_a:
TP-Link AC1900 Smart Wireless Router - Beamforming Dual Band Gigabit WiFi Internet Routers for Home, High Speed, Long Range, Ideal for Gaming (Archer C9) Got this to manage the wireless network of a family member. I'm disappointed by limitations which I describe below. After all of it, I still kept the router for it's intended purpose as I got it to work, finally.

1. You have to keep checking your configuration after you save, even if you save and reboot. On several occasions and in several different parts of the configuration, I would set a parameter and save, rebooting where necessary, only to find that the change never really got committed to the router. I saw others complain about this and I thought that maybe they just didn't notice they didn't actually hit the "save" button. Well, I can attest that this does happen as it happened to me. Sometimes it would take 3 or 4 attempts to save a parameter before it was finally committed to the router. Weird. Just don't assume you "know for sure I changed it." You have to keep checking to make sure.
2. You can't subnet off of the byte boundary (i.e., subnets other than /8, /16, or /24) without a massive performance hit. WIth nothing else on the wireless at the time, the TV had rasterization problems. For those who are really techie, please note: the 2.4GHz and 5GHz network were moved to empty channels, so no competition for performance from neighbors!
3. For the life of me, I cannot get the DHCP range of IP addresses to be anything other than what the router puts in there by default, no matter how many times I save it and reboot. To me, this is a security problem as will as a network management problem.
4. Buggy. The router worked fine when I configured it in one location. When it was time to move it to another, NOTHING had to change. When I booted the router, TCP connections would not work at all even though ICMP and UDP got through. Nothing in my router's configuration singled out TCP. Reboots did not help. I had to factory reset (full factory reset, not partial) and put in the same exact configuration. After that, TCP worked fine again. Frustrating!
5. I do not see anything about 802.11 AC speeds in the configuration despite this being an AC router (or so I thought). It only went up to 802.11n. Looking back at the Amazon listing, it lists this router as 802.11 A/C. I didn't notice the slash or maybe at the time I thought it was a typo. Now I do not. I have to look up exactly what that means. If I had devices performing at 802.11 AC now or in the future, I would have returned the router. This network is going to be fairly stagnet with the same devices for years to come.
6. I did experience the DNS problems (not resolving) that is well documented in the forums. I knew at the time that there might be a DNS resolving problem and a subnet masking problem. When I experienced the network delays along with the DNS resolver delays, I changed both the DNS configuration and the subnet masking at the same time with the intent to go back to find out which was really at fault for the DNS resolving delays. When I found the performance hit from the subnet masking, it didn't matter if it caused the DNS resolving problem (by introducing network delays on the DNS packets). I just kept the configuration as is. As such, I never went back and reverted my DNS configuration to see if the DNS resolving problem was being caused solely by the DNS configuration. I am done with the stupid problems and at that point, I didn't care just as long as the router was finally doing it's job. If you want to know what I did with the DNS: I put in OpenDNS servers as the resolvers choosing not to use the Telco's DNS resolvers because of bias in return information. When the resolving problem occurred, I simply put the Telco's DNS resolver IP's back in the configuration.

Please note: Do not forget to put in all the available firmware updates. TP-LINK just released the firmware update for the Krack vulnerability. This is a non-starter if you do not put this firmware update in! This is not a ding against the router. Although late, at least TP-Link has patched the worst wireless vulnerability in the world (yes, practically all wireless devices on earth are vulnerable unless you patch.... I'm not exaggerating either! look it up if you don't believe me.)

Other than all that, the router is now performing satisfactorily, but admittedly, the 12 wireless devices being managed are very low traffic shy of 2 streaming devices)

If you intend on using this for dd-wrt or other open source firmware (which will void your warranty), please look up the plausibility of it working. It's well documented that there is a major issue that may cause you to brick your C9 router. As such, I'm keeping this on TP-Link firmware until the warranty period is over. I'll find another router for dd-wrt with less risk.
text_fidelity_b: TP-Link AC1900 Smart Wireless Router - Beamforming Dual Band Gigabit WiFi Internet Routers for Home, High Speed, Long Range, Ideal for Gaming (Archer C9)

Fire HD 10 Tablet with Alexa, 10.1" HD Display, 16 GB, Black - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) I love everything else Amazon has ever done, so it breaks my heart to write this review. I've had a couple of iPads and they work great, but I find Apple's pricing and politics ridiculous, so I was excited to move away from them and go with an Amazon product. Sadly, the Fire HD is seriously inferior.

This device is SLOW. Every step of the setup process was painfully slow. Downloading, and even opening, apps is slow. I have my OLD iPad sitting right next to the Fire HD performing the same functions on the same WiFi connection and the Fire takes 4 times as long to do anything.

The WiFi connectivity is not great. Funny thing is, I have a Fire TV Stick running in the same room, and it has a wonderfully reliable, super-fast connection!

The touch screen is also sometimes not very responsive - I will have to tap some things 4-5 times before they trigger.

Most of the apps I was looking for are available in the Amazon App Store. However, these are buggy versions that appear to have been thrown together without the care that the developers have put into their iOs versions.

Possibly the worst part of all is the battery life. We are supposed to get 8 hours of usage.... I get about 4, even with the screen set as dim as possible. It also completely discharges on standby (with NO USE) within 2 days, even with the setting enabled to turn off WiFi when the device is on standby.

I do love the integration with the Amazon ecosystem. I hope someday Amazon will make the necessary improvements and I can give their tablets another chance. But for now, I will be returning this device with a heavy heart. :(

Brainwaves S1 - These were my least favorite, boomy and not very comfortable, heavy thick wires. The only pair of the above I returned.

What they do well - assume anything not here is more than adequate

Presentation - I feel like I'm getting what the engineer was going for in the mix. More musical than any of the above without falling into a 'warm sound'. A nice mix of forgiving and accurate. Brightness right about where it should be.
Sound Stage - Airy, instruments well placed. Center image is not the strongest, but not lacking. Does a nice job of presenting the room acoustics/reverb in the mix.
Drums - Drums are rendered very well, better than any of the the above.
Cymbals - rendered very well, especially high hat. You can tell the cymbals are made of metal, and not just the tik-tik of the drum stick tip
Treble-sibilance - Close to perfect. Nice and bright without getting into hissy/tizzy. Vocal articulation is good.
Very easy to listen to for long periods of time. They are accurate without being piercing or harsh.
Sounded good right out of the box.

Misc sound notes - distorted electric guitar is just right. They respond to EQ very well, (which the Brainwavz did not do). I really notice when something comes into the mix even if it is soft. And louder things like guitar solos, really punch in the way you hear when mixing in the studio.

If I HAD to critique the sound (this is a review) there is a very-very, (did I mention very?) lack of something in the mids. Think chest/throat area of male vocals. But this is in the realm of sound signature, a matter of taste, not a deficiency and in no way lowers my enjoyment of these.

Build - wires are thin and flexible which is what I wanted. Very nice for wearing over the ear. Microphonics close to none whether worn up or down. No hearing foot steps or wire rubbing/bouncing on clothes. Light cord/cinch is great for running.
Shape - Bullet shaped what can I say, they are light and comfortable. I like the ring of rubber around them. It gives a little grip for inserting/removing them.
I LOVE that they have a red strain relief on the right side. No having to get my glasses to see some tiny R or L printed somewhere. Cord is nice and long, which is nice for using on a treadmill or elliptical trainer, or for wearing the cord under your shirt or down in a pocket.

As much as I liked the over all presentation and frequency response I feel I should point out these are not hella flat-accurate phones (like the VC02). If a true hi-fi sound, bright/accurate/revealing, is what you are after I'd look elsewhere (maybe the VC02) Don't get me wrong, since I used to be a sound engineer, and work on electric guitars, and have very accurate/bright/revealing/fatiguing speakers on my desk, I'm very picky about good accurate sound. But that makes these musical, easy to listen to for very long periods of time and poorly recorded and/or lower quality rips won't be hard to listen to.

The title says it all - the best I've tried yet and the first phones that made me stop 'shopping' for my next pair of phones.

Listening setup. Listening has been through an amp and separate dac connected to my computer playing 192kb - 320k - FLAC music, and through my old Droid Charge (I use this because I can enable the onboard DAC) and my Samsung Note II listening to ripped music (192k or better) or Spotify/Pandora at their highest quality settings available in the premium versions.
text_fidelity_b: Nuforce NE-700X Titanium Coated In-Ear Headphones - Aqua Silver
